The Hidden Cost of Janitorial Turnover: Why Your Cleaning Company's Retention Rate Matters

The commercial cleaning industry has one of the highest turnover rates of any sector — averaging 200-400% annually according to ISSA data. This means the average cleaning company replaces its entire workforce two to four times per year. For facility managers, this statistic isn't just an industry curiosity — it directly impacts the quality, consistency, and security of your cleaning program. Understanding the turnover problem and how to evaluate a cleaning partner's retention practices is essential for any facility manager who's tired of the revolving door.

Why Turnover Is So High

Janitorial work combines several factors that drive high attrition: physically demanding labor, non-standard hours (evenings, weekends, overnight), historically low wages, limited benefits in many companies, minimal career advancement opportunities, and the perception of low-status work. The result is a workforce that frequently churns — employees leave for slightly better-paying alternatives, seasonal opportunities, or simply burn out. Companies that treat cleaning staff as interchangeable commodities perpetuate this cycle.

The Direct Impact on Your Facility

Every time a cleaning employee leaves and is replaced, your facility experiences a quality disruption. New employees don't know your building's layout, access points, alarm codes, or specific requirements. They haven't learned which areas need extra attention, where supplies are stored, or what your tenants expect. Training a new cleaner to full productivity on a specific facility takes 2-4 weeks minimum. During that period, cleaning quality drops measurably. In a company with 300% turnover, your facility might experience 3-4 new cleaning crews per year — meaning you're in a perpetual state of training and quality recovery.

Security Implications

Cleaning staff have keys, alarm codes, and unsupervised after-hours access to your facility. Every employee transition represents a security event — access credentials need to be updated, background checks need to be conducted for replacements, and there's an inherent risk period during transitions. Facilities with sensitive operations — healthcare offices with patient records, government buildings with classified areas, financial offices — face elevated risk from constant personnel changes. A cleaning company with 40% annual turnover versus 300% turnover represents a dramatically different security profile.

What to Ask Your Cleaning Company

When evaluating cleaning partners, ask directly: what is your annual employee turnover rate? Companies with genuinely low turnover will share this number proudly — it's a competitive advantage. Then ask what they do to achieve retention: do they pay above-market wages, provide health insurance, offer advancement opportunities, invest in training, and treat their employees with respect? Ask for tenure data on the specific crew that would be assigned to your facility. And ask what their protocol is when a crew member leaves — how quickly can they deploy a trained replacement, and what quality safeguards are in place during transitions?

The Retention-Quality Connection

Data from ISSA and our own operations confirm a strong correlation between employee retention and client retention. Companies with turnover under 60% typically achieve client retention rates of 90% or higher. Companies with turnover above 200% rarely sustain client retention above 75%. The mechanism is straightforward: retained employees become experts on their assigned facilities, deliver consistent quality, build relationships with building occupants, and take ownership of their work. This expertise cannot be replicated by constantly rotating new hires through your building.

GreenPoint invests in employee retention through above-market compensation, benefits, ongoing training, and a culture of respect. Our turnover rate is a fraction of the industry average, and our 98% client retention rate is the direct result.
